title: Health officials reflect on ‘lasting impact,’ heroic response following CFB Wainwright fire
summary: More than a month after a deadly fire engulfed a training range at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alberta health officials are expected to provide an update on the soldiers still recovering from…

image.caption: The burned area of Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is seen in Alberta, Canada, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Ty O'Neil/Associated Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton

More than a month after a deadly fire engulfed a training range at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alberta health officials are expected to provide an update on the soldiers still recovering from the flames.
19 soldiers still being cared for in provincial hospitals, with 7 listed in critical condition
Senior Alberta health officials are expressing their gratitude to the front-line health workers who rushed to care for soldiers injured in the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

During a news conference Thursday, stark new details emerged about how the disaster unfolded inside Alberta hospitals. Health officials provided new insight into how the surge of patients has tested and will continue to test the strength of the health-care system and the severely wounded soldiers.

The mass casualty disaster triggered a system-wide response of rare scope and scale, and the complex medical needs of the service members who were most severely injured are expected to create a lasting strain.
'Extraordinary demands'

Dr. Josh Wong, interim medical director of the Firefighters' Burn Treatment Unit at the University of Alberta Hospital, said at the news conference that his ward was overwhelmed in the immediate aftermath of the Oct. 17 tragedy.
He recalled that, within a matter of hours, 20 severely wounded soldiers were brought to the burn unit in Edmonton, pushing the ward to more than five times its normal capacity.
Faced with an impossible equation, hospital staff diverted patients to other departments across the hospital, including the ICU, to make room for those most wounded.

items: Specialized burn treatments deployed for soldiers injured in Alberta military base fire

blocks.text: Meanwhile, a code orange was called in hospitals across Edmonton, formally declaring that the system was nearly overwhelmed. As the community of Wainwright’s emergency room was quickly overwhelmed, patients were being airlifted to hospitals across the province.
“It's not often that we see an event like this, or at least at this magnitude, on our burn unit,” Wong said during Thursday's news conference.
“The number of patients requiring highly specialized care — complex care — placed extraordinary demands on our teams, both in the burn unit as well as in intensive care and on the ward.”

items: Family of injured Wainwright soldier holds bedside vigil in burn unit

blocks.text: Military officials have said that on the afternoon of Oct. 17, a low-burning grass fire flared suddenly in a fierce windstorm and rapidly advanced on soldiers involved in a training exercise at the base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.
Four soldiers were killed as the flames spread. A fifth soldier succumbed to his injuries in an Ontario hospital on Nov. 13.
As the training field was evacuated and the flames spread beyond the base, 39 people were initially taken to hospital, many with severe burns.

And Wong said, for many of them, their injuries will be life-altering. Wong — who also serves as a burn, plastic and reconstructive surgeon — said recovering from such severe burns can take months, even years.

items: Fifth soldier dead from injuries suffered in CFB Wainwright fire, officials say

blocks.text: Such patients often require multiple surgical procedures along with prolonged physical and psychological therapy.
Wong cautioned that the psychological scars often become more pronounced once the physical wounds have healed.
“Their care doesn't end when they leave the ICU or even the hospital,” Wong said.
“Our focus remains on providing specialized care to these patients who are in need, supporting their families and helping them through every stage of their recovery.”

items: How soldiers from Wainwright are recovering in Edmonton

blocks.text: During Thursday's news conference, Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim chief executive officer for Acute Care Alberta, said much of the work of Alberta's health-care workers in the wake of the disaster went unseen.
She said teams across the province managed the tragedy with grace under immense pressure.
All parts of the health-care system worked in tandem to ensure soldiers received the care they needed, she said.
“I am incredibly proud of every single person who stepped up in this crisis.”

Acute Care Alberta said 19 soldiers were still being cared for in provincial hospitals as of Tuesday, with seven listed in critical condition. Military officials said as of Saturday, others were also being cared for in hospitals in British Columbia and Ontario.

items: Canadian Armed Forces sending nurses to Alberta to help treat CFB Wainwright survivors

blocks.text: Three investigations are examining the circumstances of the fire, including the cause and spread, as well as why the live-fire training exercise continued as fierce winds whipped the flames across the base.

During Thursday's news conference, Michael Suddes, interim COO of the Edmonton Corridor for Alberta Health Services, said his thoughts remain with the families of the soldiers who lost their lives and the patients still recovering from their injuries.
He said the disaster has undoubtedly also left a lasting mark on first responders, health-care workers and volunteers who were called to help those injured in the flames.
“We know these experiences can stay with responders, and we recognize the lasting impact that an event of this magnitude carries,” he said.
“Not only for those who provided life-saving measures in the immediate minutes and hours of the incident, but the teams who continue to deliver critical care for weeks and months and years.”
